did_you_know.text: The chapter opens by inviting the islands and nations to stand before the Lord for judgment. The nations are called to gather strength, draw near, and speak.
The Lord is presented as the one who acts throughout all generations: he “calls the generations from the beginning,” and is the First and the Last, emphasizing his control over history.
The nations try to strengthen themselves through cooperation among craftsmen: the craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and they even fasten the idol with nails so that it will not fall.
Israel is described by three titles that connect the nation to the patriarchal tradition: “my servant,” “Jacob whom you have chosen,” and “the offspring of Abraham my friend.”
The Lord repeats his promise to help Israel in several ways: he will strengthen them, help them, support them, and hold them with his righteous right hand.
Israel’s image changes from “Jacob, a worm” into a sharp, new threshing sledge with double-edged blades—a farming tool used to thresh and break up grain.
The Lord promises to answer the poor and needy when they seek water, emphasizing: “I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.”

At the center of the description of redemption, the wilderness is transformed into a place of water: rivers flow over the barren heights, springs appear in the valleys, and the parched land becomes a place of springs.

The water is accompanied by a transformation of the vegetation: cedars, acacias, myrtles, and olive trees will grow in the wilderness, while cypresses, plane trees, and box trees will appear in the desert plain. The purpose of this transformation is that people may recognize the Lord’s work.

The Lord challenges the idols to present their arguments and reveal what happened in the past and what will happen in the future. Since they cannot do so, their works are described as “wind and emptiness.”
